title: GROUPING SETS/ROLLUP/CUBE, DISTINCT ON
summary: GROUPING SETS computes several GROUP BYs in one pass: ROLLUP adds subtotals along a hierarchy, CUBE every combination, and GROUPING() tells a subtotal's NULL from a NULL in the data. DISTINCT ON, a PostgreSQL extension, keeps the first row of each group in ORDER BY order.

examples.title: ROLLUP subtotals, and GROUPING() to label them

annotations.note: ROLLUP (suite, browser) means GROUPING SETS ((suite, browser), (suite), ()): every prefix of the list, which fits a hierarchy (browsers within a suite). One query returns 5 detail rows, 3 suite subtotals and the grand total.

A column that isn't part of a row's grouping set comes back NULL. auth now has two rows with browser NULL: the API tests (2 runs, 70 ms) and the suite subtotal (4 runs, 530 ms). Without GROUPING(browser) in the ORDER BY, even their relative order would be unspecified.

GROUPING(browser) = 1 marks the rolled-up rows, so coalesce only ever sees the NULLs that came from the data. A plain coalesce(browser, 'all browsers') would have labelled the API tests as a subtotal.

With several arguments GROUPING returns a bitmask, rightmost argument in the lowest bit, 1 meaning "not grouped here": 0 is a detail row, 1 a suite subtotal, 3 the grand total. ROLLUP never produces 2 (browser without suite); CUBE does.

Sorting on GROUPING() places each subtotal after its details and the total last, whatever NULL ordering is in effect. suite and browser here are the input columns, not the labels, which would sort 'all suites' among the real names.

examples.title: GROUPING SETS instead of UNION ALL, CUBE, and the one-scan plan

annotations.note: Each set in the list is an independent GROUP BY: per suite, per status, and () for the total. The docs define it as the UNION ALL of those queries, with NULL in the columns a set doesn't use.
CUBE (suite, status) expands to all four subsets, so it adds the per-status totals (level 2) that ROLLUP leaves out. With n columns that is 2^n groupings; CUBE of five columns asks for 32.
MixedAggregate: one Seq Scan feeds a hash table per column (Hash Key: suite, Hash Key: status) plus a running total for (). The UNION ALL spelling would scan test_runs three times.

examples.title: DISTINCT ON: the latest run per test case, ties, and the portable alternative

annotations.note: Two runs of Export in the same second: a tie on ran_at. Real data has these (retries, batch imports), and they decide whether the query is deterministic.

DISTINCT ON (test_case) keeps the first row of each test_case group in ORDER BY order. The leading ORDER BY items must be the DISTINCT ON expressions; the ones after them pick the winner: newest ran_at, and for the tie the higher id. Drop id DESC and the docs call the chosen row unpredictable.
The inner ORDER BY is tied to the DISTINCT ON groups. To present the winners in a different order, wrap the query and sort outside.

row_number() (window functions get their own module) numbers the rows of each partition in the given order, and rn = 1 keeps the first. It is standard SQL, and it turns into "latest three per test" with rn <= 3, which DISTINCT ON can't do.
SQLSTATE 42P10. The sort would order rows by ran_at alone, so rows of one test case aren't adjacent and "first of the group" has no meaning.

use_cases: Report exports with subtotals and a grand total: per suite and browser, per suite, overall (ROLLUP)
Dashboard tiles that each need a different breakdown (per status, per suite, total) from one query (GROUPING SETS)
Cross-tab margins: row totals, column totals and the corner total (CUBE over two columns)
Latest row per key with DISTINCT ON: last run per test, current price per product, newest address per customer
strengths: Several groupings come out of one scan of the data; the UNION ALL equivalent reads the table once per grouping
GROUPING() distinguishes subtotal rows from NULLs in the data, which no amount of coalesce can
DISTINCT ON returns whole rows, not just the max: the latest run's status, duration and id together, without joining max(ran_at) back to the table
Grouping sets, ROLLUP, CUBE and multi-argument GROUPING are standard SQL (features T431-T434 in PostgreSQL's conformance list)
weaknesses: Result rows have different meanings in one column set, so every consumer must check GROUPING() or a level column
CUBE grows as 2^n; a few extra columns produce far more groupings than anyone reads
DISTINCT ON is a PostgreSQL extension and only keeps one row per group; top-N needs row_number() or LATERAL
DISTINCT ON sorts its whole input (or reads an index in that order); with few keys and many rows each, LATERAL ... LIMIT 1 over an index reads far less

pitfalls.title: Labelling subtotals with coalesce
pitfalls.detail: coalesce(browser, 'all') can't tell a subtotal's NULL from a NULL in the data, so detail rows get mislabelled as totals. Test GROUPING().
pitfalls.good: CASE WHEN GROUPING(browser) = 1 THEN 'all browsers' ELSE coalesce(browser, 'api') END

pitfalls.title: DISTINCT ON without a complete tie-breaker
pitfalls.detail: When two rows tie on every ORDER BY item after the DISTINCT ON expressions, either may be kept, and the answer can change between runs. End the ORDER BY with a unique column.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) * FROM test_runs ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC
pitfalls.good: SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) * FROM test_runs ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC, id DESC

pitfalls.title: Combining ROLLUPs repeats grouping sets
pitfalls.detail: Several grouping items multiply into their Cartesian product, so GROUP BY ROLLUP (a, b), ROLLUP (a, c) contains (a, b) and (a, c) twice and (a) three times, and their rows repeat accordingly. GROUP BY DISTINCT (PG 14) removes the duplicate sets.
pitfalls.bad: GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser), ROLLUP (suite, status)
pitfalls.good: GROUP BY DISTINCT ROLLUP (suite, browser), ROLLUP (suite, status)

pitfalls.title: Expecting the subtotal rows in the right place
pitfalls.detail: Without ORDER BY, grouping-set rows come out in whatever order the plan produces them. Sort on GROUPING() and the grouping columns explicitly.

quiz.q: Which grouping sets does `GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser)` compute?
quiz.why: ROLLUP takes every prefix of its list, down to the empty set. All subsets, including (browser) alone, is CUBE.

quiz.q: A ROLLUP result row has browser NULL. How do you tell whether it is a subtotal?
quiz.why: GROUPING(browser) is 1 only when browser is not part of the row's grouping set; a NULL in the data gives 0.

quiz.q: What does GROUPING(suite, status) return on the grand-total row?
quiz.why: Neither column is grouped, so both bits are set: 2 for suite plus 1 for status.

quiz.q: What happens with `SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, passed FROM test_runs ORDER BY ran_at DESC`?
options: It returns the latest run per test case
It fails: the DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions
It returns one arbitrary run per test case
quiz.why: DISTINCT ON relies on the sort placing each group's rows together, so the ORDER BY must start with test_case (SQLSTATE 42P10).

body:
## Concept

A report rarely wants just one level of summary. It wants runs per suite and browser,
per suite, and overall. Plain `GROUP BY` gives one level per query. **Grouping sets**
(PG 9.5) give several in one result:

- `GROUPING SETS ((a), (b), ())` lists the groupings explicitly. Each set behaves like
  its own `GROUP BY`, and its rows have NULL in the columns the set doesn't use.
- `ROLLUP (a, b)` is shorthand for every prefix, `(a, b), (a), ()`: subtotals down a
  hierarchy.
- `CUBE (a, b)` is shorthand for every subset, `(a, b), (a), (b), ()`: the margins of a
  cross-tab.
- `GROUPING(a, b)` returns a bitmask saying which columns are rolled up in the current
  row, so a subtotal's NULL can be told from a NULL in the data.

**DISTINCT ON** answers a different summary question: not "how many per group" but
"which row per group". `SELECT DISTINCT ON (key) ... ORDER BY key, preference` keeps the
first row of each key in that order: the latest run per test case, with all its
columns. It is a PostgreSQL extension; `row_number()` is the standard equivalent.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Spreadsheets and BI tools:** a pivot table with subtotals and a grand total is
  `ROLLUP`; "totals for rows and columns" is `CUBE` over the two pivot axes.
- **Python:** pandas `pivot_table(..., margins=True)` adds the `All` row and column, as
  `CUBE` over two columns does. "First row per group" is
  `df.sort_values(...).drop_duplicates('test_case')`, which keeps the first occurrence:
  the same sort-then-keep-first algorithm as `DISTINCT ON`.
- **Java, JS, Go:** you would run one grouping pass per level, or add subtotals in a
  second loop. Grouping sets compute every level from one scan.
- **JS:** latest per key is usually a `reduce` into a `Map` that replaces an entry when a
  newer one arrives. That compares two rows at a time; `DISTINCT ON` sorts once and keeps
  the first of each run of equal keys.

## How it works

`GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((suite), (status), ())` is defined as the `UNION ALL` of three
queries: `GROUP BY suite` with `status` as NULL, `GROUP BY status` with `suite` as NULL,
and the ungrouped total. The executor computes them together: example 2's plan is one
scan feeding a hash table per set (`MixedAggregate`).

Grouping items combine as a Cartesian product: `GROUP BY suite, ROLLUP (browser,
status)` means `GROUPING SETS ((suite, browser, status), (suite, browser), (suite))`.
That is how you get subtotals *within* each suite without a grand total.

`DISTINCT ON` runs after the sort: rows arrive ordered by the `DISTINCT ON` expressions
first, and a `Unique` step keeps the first row of each run of equal keys. That is why
the `ORDER BY` must start with those expressions.

## Design notes

Use grouping sets when the database is the reporting engine: CSV exports, admin
summaries, dashboard tiles. Always return `GROUPING()` (or a level column derived from
it) so the consumer never has to guess what a NULL means, and always sort explicitly.
Prefer `GROUPING SETS` that list exactly the levels you need over `CUBE`, which grows as
2^n.

For "one row per group", pick by shape. `DISTINCT ON` is the shortest when you need
one row per key and run on PostgreSQL only; always end its `ORDER BY` with a unique
column. `row_number()` is portable and extends to top-N. When there are few keys and
many rows per key, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... ORDER BY ran_at DESC LIMIT 1)` over an index
on `(test_case, ran_at DESC)` reads one index entry per key instead of every row (see the
LATERAL lesson).

files.examples/01_rollup.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.aggregation.grouping-sets): several groupings in one pass; GROUPING() tells them apart.
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  browser     text,             -- NULL: an API test, no browser involved
  duration_ms int NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'chrome', 120), (2, 'auth', 'firefox', 340),
  (3, 'auth',   NULL,      30), (4, 'auth', NULL,       40),
  (5, 'export', 'chrome', 900), (6, 'search', 'chrome', 80);

-- Detail rows, a subtotal per suite and a grand total, in one query.
-- Look at auth: two rows with browser NULL that mean different things.
SELECT suite, browser, count(*) AS runs, sum(duration_ms) AS total_ms
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser)
ORDER BY suite, browser, GROUPING(browser);

-- GROUPING(col) is 1 where col was rolled up, so a subtotal's NULL can be
-- told apart from a NULL in the data. The two-argument form is a bitmask.
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(suite) = 1 THEN 'all suites' ELSE suite END
         AS suite_label,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(browser) = 1 THEN 'all browsers'
            ELSE coalesce(browser, 'api') END AS browser_label,
       GROUPING(suite, browser) AS level,
       count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY ROLLUP (suite, browser)
ORDER BY GROUPING(suite), suite, GROUPING(browser), browser;
files.examples/02_sets_cube.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_runs (id int PRIMARY KEY, suite text NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth', 'passed'), (2, 'auth', 'failed'), (3, 'auth', 'passed'),
  (4, 'search', 'failed'), (5, 'search', 'failed');

-- Two unrelated breakdowns and the total, as one result. Without grouping
-- sets this is three GROUP BY queries glued together with UNION ALL.
SELECT suite, status, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((suite), (status), ())
ORDER BY GROUPING(suite, status), suite, status;

-- CUBE (a, b) is every subset: (a, b), (a), (b) and ().
SELECT GROUPING(suite, status) AS level, suite, status, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY CUBE (suite, status)
ORDER BY level, suite, status;

-- One scan of the table feeds all the groupings.
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT suite, status, count(*)
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((suite), (status), ());
files.examples/03_distinct_on.sql:
SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id        int PRIMARY KEY,
  test_case text NOT NULL,
  ran_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  passed    boolean NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'Login',  '2026-11-12 09:00+03', true),
  (2, 'Login',  '2026-11-13 09:00+03', false),
  (3, 'Logout', '2026-11-12 10:00+03', true),
  (4, 'Export', '2026-11-13 08:00+03', false),
  (5, 'Export', '2026-11-13 08:00+03', true);  -- a retry in the same second

-- The latest run per test case: sort so the wanted row comes first in its
-- group, and DISTINCT ON keeps only that first row.
SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, ran_at, passed, id
FROM test_runs
ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC, id DESC;

-- Want the result in another order? Sort outside.
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, ran_at, passed
  FROM test_runs
  ORDER BY test_case, ran_at DESC, id DESC
) AS latest
ORDER BY ran_at DESC, test_case;

-- The standard-SQL equivalent: number the rows per group, keep number 1.
SELECT test_case, ran_at, passed
FROM (
  SELECT test_case, ran_at, passed,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM test_runs
) AS ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY test_case;

-- The DISTINCT ON expressions must lead the ORDER BY.
SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case) test_case, passed FROM test_runs ORDER BY ran_at DESC;
